extracted.intended_audience: individual humanities scholars preparing NEH Summer Stipends applications
extracted.subtask_description: Preparing and submitting an application for the NEH Summer Stipends program: who is eligible, institutional nomination rules, required application components, and the review criteria reviewers will apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual significance of the proposed project
rubrics_metrics.description: The intellectual significance of the proposed project, including its value to scholars, students, or general audiences in the humanities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the most important criterion. Explain why the project is important and how it will change the way scholars or other readers understand the topic or do their own research. Discuss the project's contribution to scholarly discussion, how it builds on or challenges existing work, and identify the audience(s) who will benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality or promise of quality of the applicant
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality or promise of quality of the applicant as a humanities researcher and (for course revision projects) as a teacher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate your preparation to do the project: discuss previous research and publication record, language skills, relevant competencies, and access to necessary archives. For course revision, address teaching qualifications. Use the CV and narrative to show you are the right person to complete the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of conception, definition, organization, and clarity of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality of the conception, definition, organization, and description of the project and the clarity of expression in the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present a clear, well-conceived plan. Write for well-educated generalists: avoid jargon, explain technical terms, and make the project's aims and structure explicit so reviewers who are not specialists can follow the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility and appropriateness of the proposed plan of work
rubrics_metrics.description: The feasibility and appropriateness of the proposed plan of work, including, when relevant, the soundness of the dissemination and access plans for the proposed audience or audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe in as much detail as possible what you will do during the grant period and why that work is achievable in the proposed timeframe. Include realistic dissemination/access plans (how the work will reach intended audiences) and explain how the two months fit into the larger project trajectory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Likelihood that the applicant will complete the project
rubrics_metrics.description: The likelihood that the applicant will complete the project (not necessarily during the period of performance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate the current stage of the project and provide evidence (past productivity, realistic plan, access to materials, timeline) that completion is plausible. Explain how the Summer Stipends period advances completion within the broader project timeline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative must address research and contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrative should include a discussion of the project’s contribution to the scholarly discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the state of research on your topic, identify your research questions, explain how your work will build on, disagree with, or offer new interpretation, and describe the intended audience and how they will benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative must present methodology and a detailed work plan
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrative should include methodology and work plan: how you will answer your research questions and what you will do during the grant period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain methods clearly (so non-specialists can understand), specify the current stage of the project, and give a detailed, day-by-day or task-by-task account of planned activities during the two months.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative must document competencies, skills, and access
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrative should describe competencies, skills, and access that qualify the applicant to carry out the project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss previous research and publication record, relevant language skills, institutional or archival access, and any other qualifications that support feasibility and promise of quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative must specify final product and dissemination
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrative should describe the final product and dissemination plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether the product will be a book, article, edition, translation, or other interpretive tool; provide a brief outline if a book and note any publisher conversations if relevant. Explain how results will be made available to intended audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required application components and page limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications must include a three page narrative, one page bibliography, two page C.V., any necessary appendices, and names/contact info for two references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the specified page limits exactly. See program guidelines for complete details. These components should be concise and mutually supporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence across application documents
rubrics_metrics.description: The various application documents should work together; think of them as separate chapters of the same book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make sure narrative, bibliography, CV, and appendices present a consistent, reinforcing case: research questions align with methodology, bibliography supports state-of-field claims, CV demonstrates relevant experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for a broad scholarly audience; avoid unexplained jargon
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluators may or may not be specialists in the project's field; some review panels are disciplinary and others interdisciplinary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write for well-educated generalists: avoid or explain technical terms, provide necessary context so reviewers outside your specialty can evaluate significance and method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility: citizenship/residency and academic status
rubrics_metrics.description: All individuals are eligible with a few exceptions: applicants must be US citizens or residents of the US for at least three years; degree candidates are not eligible; a terminal degree is not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm citizenship/residency status and that you are not a degree candidate before applying. Independent scholars and faculty at various institutions are welcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomination requirement for tenured and tenure-track faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: Tenured and tenure-track faculty must be nominated by their institution; applications must include the name of the nominating official.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions run their own nomination processes and identify a nominating official; include that official's name in your application so NEH can confirm the nomination. This requirement aims to broaden institutional representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional nomination limits
rubrics_metrics.description: All institutions can nominate up to two people per year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate with your institution early to be selected as one of the nominees; institutions typically run internal competitions to choose nominees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions from nomination
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain categories are exempt from the institutional nomination requirement: non-tenure-track faculty (including adjuncts), staff, community college faculty, emeritus faculty, and independent scholars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you fall into an exempt category you may apply without institutional nomination; ensure you understand which category applies to you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission process and timeline (grants.gov)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications are submitted through grants.gov; register with grants.gov two weeks before the deadline and submit early.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Register and familiarize yourself with grants.gov well before the deadline. Each applicant submits their own application (not via an institutional account). The program guidelines (pp. 9-17) explain how to navigate the three forms required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use NEH guidelines, sample narratives, and funded projects database
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants should consult the program guidelines, sample narratives, and NEH's funded projects database for information and examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read the guidelines carefully (they describe eligibility, allowable costs, required materials, and evaluation). Review sample successful applications for structure and tone, but do not treat them as exact models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable project activities and expected products
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical project activities include humanities research, travel to archives, scholarly editing, writing and revision; expected products include articles, monographs, translations, editions, and other interpretive tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propose activities and products that match the two-month support period and indicate how the stipend will advance scholarly work towards those products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand competitive context
rubrics_metrics.description: Program funding statistics: five-year average received 834 applications and made 77 awards (funding rate 9%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of high competition; apply early and craft a strong case, but do not be discouraged from applying.
